segments.title: Opening: The Fog and Chancery's Shadow

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, passionate, and sometimes heated reading of one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series, we'll be moving through Charles Dickens's vast, fog-drenched masterpiece chapter by chapter.
We'll be asking what makes it still feel so alive, so urgent — and at times so uncomfortable — nearly two centuries after it was written.
Joining me today are three readers whose company I'd want in any dark room this novel leads us into.
First, Dr. Eleanor Hartley — a novelist and creative writing scholar who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism: every gear, every spring, every deliberate tick.
Then Dr. Daniel Rosen — a cultural historian for whom every courtroom, every slum, and every act of charity in this novel is a question of who holds power and who pays the price.

And finally, Ms. Caroline Woodcourt — a critic and devoted re-reader of classic fiction who knows Bleak House with the intimacy of a very old friendship and the fresh eye of someone who still finds things to gasp at.
Welcome, all three of you.
We begin today where Dickens himself begins — in the fog.
The fog of London, the fog of the law, and the fog of a chancery suit that has already swallowed generations before the first page is turned.
Eleanor, you've talked about the architecture of this novel before. Where do you want us to start?
I want to start with something that sounds Gothic and sensational but is actually one of the most precise structural statements Dickens ever made.
Late in the novel, we discover what is left of a character named Krook — a man who has been, throughout, a grotesque mirror of the Lord Chancellor himself.
He dies by spontaneous combustion. And Dickens describes what remains with this extraordinary, almost forensic calm.
The narrator says — and I think this sentence is one of the great sentences in the novel —
"Oh, horror, he IS here!"
That emphasis on IS — that italicised present tense — is doing something devastating.
The horror isn't that he's gone. The horror is that this — this ash, this char, this residue — this IS him.
That's the novel's logic in a single word: the system burns people down until only the residue of them is left. And then it calls that nothing.
And what I'd add is that the passage doesn't stop there — it insists on the larger truth.
The full line is: "this from which we run away, striking out the light and overturning one another into the street, is all that represents him."
"All that represents him." That word — represents — is a political word.
In a system that claims to represent the interests of its subjects — as Chancery claims to represent the heirs of Jarndyce — what actually gets represented is nothing.
A burnt patch. White ash. The char of a human being who was consumed by the very institution that promised to adjudicate his affairs.
What strikes me, reading that passage aloud — and I have read it aloud — is the hesitation before the horror.
The narrator asks: is it the cinder of a small charred log? Or is it coal?
That moment of not-knowing — of trying to make it be something ordinary, something explicable — makes the recognition unbearable when it comes.
And what moves me is that Krook is nobody's favourite character. He's grotesque, he's a hoarder, he's complicit in misery.
And yet Dickens insists on the full weight of his annihilation. Even Krook deserves to be mourned as a human being.
That connects to something I keep returning to with Bleak House — the way it uses what I'd call accumulative tragedy.
There's a character — Miss Flite — who appears throughout the novel as a kind of eccentric, slightly comic figure haunting the courts of Chancery.
But at one point she sits down and simply tells Esther what Chancery did to her family. And the effect is devastating.
She says — and listen to the rhythm here, the terrible repetition —
"I heard, as I had often heard before, that this was all the work of Chancery. When I got better, I went to look at the monster. And then I found out how it was, and I was drawn to stay there."
'Drawn' — that word does all the work. Father drawn. Brother drawn. Sister drawn. And then herself drawn.
It's a gravitational metaphor. Chancery as a black hole. It doesn't need to be violent. It simply pulls.
That repetition — 'drawn, drawn, drawn' — is also the novel mapping a class mechanism with almost clinical precision.
Notice how Miss Flite places each family member: father to bankruptcy and then debtors' prison, brother to drunkenness and rags, sister to something she won't name.
Each stage is a step down the social ladder. Chancery doesn't just ruin you financially. It remakes you — degrades you — at every level.
And then Miss Flite herself survives — if that's the word — as a court fixture, a human remnant, the living proof of what the system produces when it's done with you.
And there's something almost unbearable about the line: 'Hush! Never ask to what!'
She closes the door on her sister's fate entirely. We never find out. Dickens doesn't let us.
And that silence — that refusal to narrate — is itself a form of testimony. Some things, the novel suggests, are beyond the reach of what can be said in public.
Miss Flite is comic on the surface and absolutely tragic underneath. That's one of the novel's great tricks: it hides devastation inside eccentricity.
There's another passage I want to bring in here — because it speaks directly to a different kind of sacrifice that Chancery's world demands.
Jarndyce tells Esther about Lady Dedlock's sister — a woman who chose, in full knowledge and full grief, to vanish from the life of the man she loved.
And the reason is bound up in pride, in honour — in a sense of self so rigid it becomes its own kind of cage.
Jarndyce reads from her letter — or rather, conveys what it said — and the formulation is extraordinary:

"she wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did — and that the resolution was exacted from her by her knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too."
'She died to him.' That's not metaphor — the passage insists it was literal truth. She willed herself into a kind of living death.
And then the most crushing line: she 'would live in it and die in it.' She did both.
What I find remarkable about that passage is its insistence on mutuality — on the way the woman's own pride is complicit in her destruction.
'His proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too.' She isn't simply crushed by a man's code. She has internalised that code.
That's a brilliant piece of social anatomy. The ideology of honour doesn't just oppress from outside. It colonises the self.
And so the most devastating sacrifices in this world aren't forced. They're chosen — because the chooser has no other language for dignity available to her.
What stays with me is the very last line of that account: 'Nor did any one.'
Jarndyce says that Boythorn never saw her, never heard from her from that hour. 'Nor did any one.'
Three words at the end. A full stop. And a whole life is folded away into silence.
That's Dickens at his most quietly devastating — the understatement that carries more weight than any theatrical flourish could.
Ash, silence, self-immolation — we're barely through our opening passages and the novel has already given us its full range of the ways people are consumed by the world it depicts.
In our next segment, we'll be moving deeper into the machinery of Chancery itself — and asking who it serves and who it destroys.

segments.title: The Machinery of Injustice: Class and the Law

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series that takes Dickens's great labyrinthine novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with relish.
Today's segment is called The Machinery of Injustice: Class and the Law.
We're going to look at how Bleak House exposes — with extraordinary precision — the way the law, poverty, and class grind certain lives down to almost nothing.
With me today are three readers who know this novel in quite different ways.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is obsessed with the architecture of Dickens's sentences — and with good reason.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in the novel — the courts, the aristocracy, philanthropy itself — as a mechanism of class power.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong reader of Bleak House who brings an intimate, emotional intelligence to the text that I find consistently illuminating.
Let's begin with Jo — perhaps the novel's most devastating figure — and what Dickens does when the law has finished with him.
Jo appears at the inquest as a witness, and he is immediately dismissed — he can't swear an oath because he has no idea what an oath is.
The system looks at this child and says: insufficient.
But what Dickens does next is extraordinary.
Before the inquest throws Jo out, we actually hear what he would have said — what testimony the court rejected.
And it's this: the dead man, on one cold winter night, saw Jo shivering in a doorway.
"He had not a friend in the world, said, 'Neither have I. Not one!' and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging."
That's it. That is the whole weight of what Jo has to offer — and it is enormous.
What strikes me there is the grammatical shape of that passage — the way Dickens uses indirect speech to present Jo's testimony.
It's all reported: "that graceless creature only knows that..." — the narrator summarises, filters, mediates.
Which is exactly what the court did to Jo — it mediated him out of existence.
But then — and this is the move I love — inside that reported speech, the dead man's direct words burst through.
The narration sets it up, and then we hear the man himself speak — unmediated, raw.
"Neither have I. Not one!"
Three words. Sentence fragment. It's a life.
Dickens uses the law's own indifference as a formal device — and then detonates it from within.
Eleanor is right about the formal brilliance, but I want to linger on the political content of those questions Nemo asks Jo.
"Whether he slept sound at night, and how he bore cold and hunger, and whether he ever wished to die."
These are not small-talk questions. These are the questions that no institution in the novel ever asks.
The court doesn't ask. The church doesn't ask. The philanthropic societies certainly don't ask.
The only person who asks is another outcast — a man so marginalised that the law won't even name him, only calling him Nemo: no one.
Dickens is showing us that solidarity in this novel lives entirely outside the institutions designed to provide it.
And the narrator returns to Jo directly after the inquest — in one of the novel's most extraordinary passages.
Caroline, you've spoken about reading this aloud — what happens when you do?
It's almost unbearable to read aloud. Dickens turns to address Jo directly — second person, present tense.
"Jo, is it thou?" — and that archaic "thou" is doing so much work.
It's tender. It's biblical. It elevates a crossing-sweeper to the register of the Psalms.
And then comes this extraordinary sentence about what Jo does carry, despite everything.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
The spelling. "Wos wery." Dickens keeps Jo's dialect — doesn't correct it, doesn't translate it.
That gratitude, in Jo's own garbled speech, is the ray of light. Not grace from above — grace from below.
The address to Jo is a structural rupture in the novel — suddenly the omniscient narrator steps entirely out of the fiction.
It's almost the narrator saying: the novel cannot contain this. This requires direct speech. Direct accusation.
The phrase "though a rejected witness" — Dickens is holding the court's verdict up to the light and finding it monstrous.
The law rejected him. The narrator refuses to. That's the whole argument.
I agree — and I'd add that Dickens frames this with extraordinary precision: Jo is "not quite in outer darkness."
Not saved. Not celebrated. Just — not quite in outer darkness.
That's a very precise account of what the system leaves a child like Jo with.
Not destruction — just the bare minimum of not-quite-destruction.
Now, compare that with Mrs. Piper's testimony at the same inquest — because Dickens also gives us a comic vision of how rumour substitutes for fact.
Eleanor, you've noted that Dickens's comedy is never merely decorative — what's happening in Mrs. Piper's speech?
Mrs. Piper is one of those passages that looks like pure comic relief and is actually a precision instrument.
Dickens gives her this unstoppable parenthetical style — clauses breeding inside clauses, never arriving at a point.
The narrator tells us she has "a good deal to say, chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation, but not much to tell."
That distinction — much to say, not much to tell — is the entire critique of the inquest system in one line.
The court fills itself with this kind of testimony and calls it due process.
And she keeps calling the deceased "the plaintive" — as if he's the one making a complaint, which is delicious.
The narrator notes that "the plaintive — so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased — was reported to have sold himself."
He's sold himself. She heard it from someone. Who? Well — it originatinin from his air.
The misspelling is not accidental — Dickens is rendering her verbal imprecision on the page.
This is what passes for evidence. This is what gets admitted.
And notice who does get heard. Mrs. Piper — a cabinet-maker's wife from the court — is admitted, is given the floor.
Jo, who actually knew the dead man, who has direct evidence of his character, is thrown out.
The law doesn't filter for truth. It filters for a certain kind of social legibility.
Mrs. Piper can swear an oath. She exists, legally. Jo does not.
Daniel, I want to bring you to a very different kind of scene — the Smallweed family, and what they tell us about class stripped of all sentiment.
Because if Jo is the system's victim, the Smallweeds are in some ways its spiritual product.
The Smallweeds are one of Dickens's most savage satirical inventions, and they operate on a single principle: accumulation.
Old Smallweed is reminiscing about Bart's dead father — and even grief is expressed entirely in the language of money and capital.
Listen to this: the old man says his son might have been worth a deal of money —

"just as he was beginning to build up the house that he had been making the foundations for, through many a year — you jade of a magpie, jackdaw, and poll-parrot, what do you mean! — he took ill and died of a low fever."
The eulogy for a dead son — interrupted twice by abuse hurled at the old grandmother.
The comedy is grotesque, but the point is exact: in this family, human beings are investment vehicles.
When the investment fails — through illness, through death — the grief is expressed as a balance-sheet loss.
The formal device is brilliant — Dickens runs the interrupted speech without explaining it.
We just get these abrupt swerves mid-sentence: tenderness, invective, back to tenderness.
It's almost musical — a cantata where the fugue subject is cruelty.
And the word "sparing" used about the dead father — "always being a sparing and a spare man" — is doing double duty.
Sparing as in frugal, spare as in thin. Dickens wants us to see the body shaped by the ideology.
What I find almost unbearable in that passage is the grandmother.
She's described as holding communication with nothing on earth but the trivets — she's entirely absent from herself.
The abuse lands on her and she can't even register it. She is furniture. She is the cushion that gets thrown.
After all the noise about what great men could have built with their money — here's what the family system actually built.
Let's shift now to Chesney Wold and another kind of class pressure — the pressure that falls even on those who hold power.
Daniel, you have two connected passages here — Mrs. Rouncewell's plea to Lady Dedlock, and then George alone in the great house.
Mrs. Rouncewell is the loyal housekeeper — she has given her entire life to the Dedlock family.
And here she is, pleading for her son's life — begging the mistress she has served without question to help clear him.
What she says is extraordinarily self-aware. She knows exactly what the class distance is. She names it.

"My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves."
She's not angry. She's not naive. She understands that Lady Dedlock has "proud or angry reasons" — she's acknowledging the power differential even as she begs.
That is what a lifetime of service produces: a perfect literacy in the language of your own subordination.
The phrase "you are by nature so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child" — that broke me the first time I read it.
She's not blaming Lady Dedlock. She's explaining the situation, almost gently.
You are by nature high and distant — as if that's just a feature of the world, like weather.
But of course it's not nature. It's a social arrangement that has been so thoroughly naturalized that even the victim of it speaks of it as nature.
Dickens frames Mrs. Rouncewell's speech as "genuine simplicity" — and that phrase is doing delicate work.
It's not naivety — this woman is acute. It's a simplicity of motive: she wants her son.
Against all the baroque complexity of Chancery, of aristocratic secrets, of legal maneuver — one woman wants her son not to be hanged.
Dickens is very good at putting the simple human demand up against the institutional complexity — and watching the complexity fail to answer it.
And then George patrols that same great house alone — and the passage is extraordinary in its bleakness.
He's thinking of the murdered man, the disappeared Lady, the stricken Sir Leicester. The whole social edifice has collapsed.
Dickens writes that George reflects how he MIGHT see something — that word is emphasised — which it would tax his boldness to walk up to.
"But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below, while he goes up the great staircase again, blank as the oppressive silence."
Blank. Three times. The great house has nothing left to offer — no meaning, no story, no presence.
This is what the aristocratic order looks like from the inside when the secrets that sustained it have been stripped away.
Blank as the darkness above and below — that triple repetition is almost liturgical in its cadence.

What strikes me, bringing all of this together, is how Dickens moves across class registers — from Jo in his doorway to the empty grandeur of Chesney Wold — and the same machinery is running in each place.
Different victims, different scales — but the same engine of indifference.
We'll carry this thread into the next segment, where we look at how Bleak House constructs its narrators — and what that double voice tells us about who gets to speak and who gets silenced.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
I'm joined today by three brilliant readers of this novel, each bringing a different lens to the text.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens like a fellow craftsman — always watching how the machinery works.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who treats the novel as an anatomy of class power — every institution, every wasted life, evidence of a system at work.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel who cares deeply about what it actually feels like to read these pages.
Today we're looking at Richard Carstone — his early promise, his gathering restlessness, and the first signs of the obsession that will consume him.
Eleanor, you've always been fascinated by how Dickens constructs a character's decline from the very first scenes — what do you see happening here?
What's so remarkable is that Richard's deterioration isn't announced — it's embedded in the texture of what he says.
There's a moment in chapter seventeen that I keep returning to, where Richard tries to explain himself to Esther.
He says: "I don't know how it is; I seem to want something or other to stand by."
That phrase — 'something to stand by' — is doing enormous structural work.
Richard can't name what he lacks, which is precisely the point.
Dickens gives us a character who diagnoses his own inconstancy with total accuracy, and yet the diagnosis changes nothing.
That gap between self-knowledge and self-correction is the engine of his tragedy.
And it breaks your heart, because he's not lying to Esther — or to Ada.
He goes on in that same passage with something that stops me every time I read it.
"Even you have no idea how fond I am of Ada (my darling cousin, I love you, so much!), but I don't settle down to constancy in other things."
That parenthesis — 'my darling cousin, I love you, so much!' — is almost unbearable.
He's declaring his love in the middle of confessing he can't sustain anything.
The sincerity is real and the failure is real and they coexist in a single sentence.
I want to hold onto that word — constancy — because Jarndyce uses it too, and the contrast is illuminating.
In chapter thirteen, Jarndyce offers Richard what sounds like fatherly wisdom, but it's actually a quite precise moral demand.
He tells him:
"Constancy in love is a good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy in every kind of effort."
That is not comfort — that is a verdict.
And what's striking is that Jarndyce delivers it before Richard has truly failed at anything.
The novel already knows what Richard doesn't yet know about himself.
That's exactly right, and it points to something architecturally brilliant about these early chapters.
Jarndyce's speech is essentially a prospectus for Richard's future — every warning maps onto a failure we'll later witness.
He even says: "if you entertain the supposition that any real success... ever was or could be... wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here."
'Fits and starts' — that phrase alone is Richard's entire biography condensed into three words.
The army, then medicine, then the law — each entered with a burst of enthusiasm, each abandoned when the effort becomes real.
Medicine is particularly interesting because we get an outside observer there — Mrs. Badger, who sees Richard very clearly.
Caroline, how does that passage work for you as a reader?
Mrs. Badger is one of Dickens's most underrated diagnostic voices in this novel.
She's comic in some scenes, but here she speaks with real precision.
She tells Esther that Richard 'feels languid about the profession' and that 'it is a tiresome pursuit' to him.
'Languid' is such a precise word — not hostile, not confused, just... drained of interest before the work has even begun.
And then she introduces the contrast with Woodcourt, and it's devastating.
She says young men like Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do
"will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
The reward she describes is barely a reward at all — work, poverty, disappointment — and yet for Woodcourt it's enough, because the calling is genuine.
That contrast does something important ideologically, though.
The novel sets up vocation — genuine inner calling — as the moral answer to Richard's drift.
But we should ask what Dickens doesn't examine: Richard is an orphan dependent on Chancery for his inheritance, with no income, no family connections, no established path.
His restlessness isn't simply a character flaw — it's what the system produces when it suspends a young man indefinitely between expectation and nothing.
And we see how completely Chancery has colonised his thinking when he explains why he wants to study law.
"If I went into Kenge's office... I should have my eye on the—hum!—the forbidden ground—and should be able to study it, and master it."
The profession is merely a vehicle for the obsession.
The suit has already swallowed him before he's even entered it formally.
That 'hum!' is extraordinary — Esther is transcribing Richard's actual hesitation, his momentary self-censorship.
He knows he's not supposed to talk about the suit directly — Jarndyce has effectively made it forbidden ground — and yet it erupts through anyway.
The parenthetical dash and 'hum' is Dickens showing us the repression and the compulsion simultaneously in a single punctuation mark.
That is craft operating at the level of the individual character rather than mere plot mechanics.
And what makes it all more poignant is how much Ada loves him through all of this.
Esther actually tries to use Ada's love as a lever to make Richard serious.
She tells him it was a part of his affectionate consideration for Ada
"not to slight the importance of a step that might influence both their lives."
And it works — briefly — it makes him 'almost grave.'
'Almost grave.' Not grave — almost.
That single qualifier contains everything about Richard Carstone.
And let's not overlook what Jarndyce says to both of them in chapter thirteen — which is equally important.
He says to Richard and Ada, tenderly, that if their love changes, they mustn't be ashamed.
He tells them:
"don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
Now, on the surface that's generosity — but what Jarndyce is also doing is withdrawing any external moral authority over Richard's choices.
He says explicitly: 'I have no power over you whatever.'
And that absence of external constraint — combined with Chancery's hollow promise — leaves Richard with nothing to push against.
The very kindness of Bleak House — the household — becomes a kind of enabling vacuum.
That's a genuinely uncomfortable reading — and I think it's right.
Jarndyce constructs himself as the ideal guardian — permissive, loving, non-judgmental — and the novel quietly questions whether that's enough.
Richard needs resistance, not just refuge.
And the novel is too honest to pretend that affection alone can supply what a young man without vocation, without income, and without direction genuinely needs.
And all of that — the inconstancy, the obsession, the kindness that can't quite save him — is already fully present in these early chapters.
Richard's tragedy is not a sudden fall — it's a slow gravitational pull that we can already feel from the first time he says 'I seem to want something or other to stand by.'
In our next segment, we'll be turning to Esther herself — the narrator at the heart of all this — and asking what it costs her to be the one who sees so clearly.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great sprawling masterpiece and opens it up, room by room.
I'm your host, and today we're in the thick of the novel's most unsettling comedy — the place where laughter and dread share the same sentence.
We call this segment Comic Eccentrics and Moral Chaos — and the title earns itself, I promise.
Joining me today are three readers who know this novel with a kind of devotion that I find genuinely inspiring.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing scholar who cares passionately about how Dickens builds his effects — the architecture behind the apparent chaos.
Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in the novel — the law, philanthropy, respectability itself — as a system of power.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived inside this novel for years and comes to it always as a reader first — alert to what's funny, what's heartbreaking, and what stops you cold.
Let's begin with a figure who appears almost as a joke and turns out to be something far more terrible — the old woman in Chancery.
The first time I read this woman's appearance I laughed — and then felt immediately ashamed of laughing.
Richard calls her mad, and she turns on him — so quickly, Dickens says, that he was quite abashed.
And then she tells him: she was a ward herself.
What she says next is one of the most devastating little speeches in the whole novel.
"I was not mad at that time. I had youth and hope. I believe, beauty. It matters very little now. Neither of the three served or saved me."
Three things — youth, hope, beauty — that should protect a young woman, and none of them did.
And then the speech tips into what sounds like madness — but is it?
"I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents. I expect a judgment. Shortly. On the Day of Judgment."
That final pivot — from Chancery's judgment to the Last Judgment — is either lunacy or the most logical conclusion anyone in the novel draws.
What I keep noticing is the punctuation Dickens uses for her voice — those full stops after each fragment.
"I have the honour to attend court regularly. With my documents." — each clause sealed off, self-contained, like entries in a legal brief.
The syntax is performing the system itself — Chancery reduces everything to fragments that never cohere into a verdict.
And then she says she's discovered that the sixth seal in Revelation is the Great Seal of Chancery — which has been open a long time.
That's not madness — that's typology. She's reading the system as scripture, and she's not entirely wrong.
Dickens lets her be funny and prophetic in the same breath, which is an extraordinarily difficult thing to pull off.
The detail Caroline caught — that she had youth, hope, and beauty — matters enormously in political terms.
Those are precisely the social currencies a woman in her position was supposed to trade on. And Chancery consumed all three.
She is what Richard Carstone will become if we follow the novel to its conclusion. She is the system's product.
Richard laughs at her — calls her mad — and Dickens makes absolutely sure we feel the horror of that laughter.
The people the law destroys get called eccentric. It's a very useful label for those who benefit from the system.
Daniel, that connection to Richard is exactly right — and Dickens gives us a passage that almost mirrors this one, just heartbreakingly tender instead of comic.
Just after Richard and Ada confess their love to Esther, we watch them walk away through a sunlit room.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
And then — and this is the sentence that undoes me every single time —
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
That is Esther — and Dickens — predicting the whole of Richard's fate in one cloud passing over the sun.
The craft there is almost shockingly economical for a novelist who gets accused of sprawl.
Three times he uses the word "so" — "so young, so beautiful, so full of hope" — and that repetition is doing structural work, not decorative work.
It builds the height from which they'll fall. You can't take the fall away from the reader because you've already made them feel the height.
And the turn is so quiet — "it was only a burst of light." Only. That adverb is devastating.
Esther's narration does this constantly — it retroactively shadows joyful scenes.
But I want to hold onto the love scene itself for a moment — the passage where Richard and Ada confide their love to Esther.
Esther reports that they seemed to have fallen in love with her instead of one another — because they were so confiding and so trustful.
And then she says something that I think reveals the whole structure of feeling around this relationship.
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
Esther enjoys it. She is not simply the sober moral guardian — she's swept up in it too.
And what follows is the counter-pressure: the love can only come to happiness if it inspires constancy, fortitude, and perseverance — each always for the other's sake.
Dickens places the whole burden of surviving the system on individual moral resolution — and we already know that won't be enough.
And then we get Vholes — who is the system made flesh, and also one of the funniest characters in the book in the darkest possible way.
He is asked about Ada — whether she is an eligible young lady — and what he says is extraordinary.
"As to beauty, I am not a judge of that myself, and I never did give much attention to it from a boy, but I dare say the young lady is equally eligible in that point of view."
And then — and I love this — he explains how he knows: the clerks in the Inn have assessed her, and it is, he says, a point more in their way than in mine.
Beauty has been outsourced to junior legal staff. That is Vholes's relationship to the human world.
The phrase "highly genteel young lady" — he uses it twice in the same passage — is doing something very specific.
Genteel is the language of class respectability, not human worth. Vholes is translating Ada into a category he can process professionally.
And every time he reaches something he can't quite categorise — beauty, love, happiness — he deflects it to someone else's jurisdiction.
The clerks in the Inn. Someone more qualified. It's a comic manoeuvre, but it's also a portrait of a man with no interiority whatsoever.
Vholes also invokes his duty to Mr. C's connexions every time he says something that serves only himself.
He throws out the remark about Ada's ill-advised marriage — his phrase — and then immediately says he raises it only as a duty he owes to Mr. C's connexions.
Duty. Connexions. Responsibility to the family. These are the words that respectable exploitation always travels with.
Vholes is only funny because Dickens has made his predation so perfectly legible — he is what the system produces when it produces a lawyer.
What strikes me, listening to all three of you, is how consistent Dickens is in this — the comedy and the horror occupy the same space.
The old woman in Chancery is funny and then devastating. Vholes is funny and then chilling. Richard and Ada are tender and then shadowed before they've even left the room.
Dickens doesn't let you settle into any single mode of feeling — and perhaps that's the deepest discomfort the novel creates.
In our next segment, we'll follow that discomfort further — into the fog of institutions and the people trapped inside them.

segments.title: Lady Dedlock's Hidden Life: Secrets and Shame

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and with proper attention to what makes it extraordinary.

I'm your host, and today we're descending into one of the novel's most tightly held secrets: Lady Dedlock's hidden past, and the extraordinary chain of revelation that Dickens constructs across these chapters.
With me today are three voices I'm delighted to have around this table.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose real passion is the architecture of fiction — how great writers build their effects sentence by sentence.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as documents of power — where institutions, guilt, and class operate as a system, not a backdrop.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since adolescence and brings that particular intimacy — the reader who knows every sentence and still finds new things in it.
We're looking at the moment Jarndyce tells Esther the truth of her origins, and then the uncanny first meeting between Esther and Lady Dedlock.
Eleanor, let's start with the letter. Jarndyce describes receiving this extraordinary communication nine years before. What does Dickens do with that framing?
What strikes me immediately is the restraint of that delivery — Jarndyce pauses to think before he speaks, and that pause is doing structural work.
Dickens is signalling to the reader: what follows has weight. It has been carried for nine years.
And then the letter itself is described in the most charged terms — listen to this.
"It was written to me, perhaps because it was the writer's idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to justify it."
That parallel construction — the writer's idiosyncrasy, his capacity to justify it — is making the relationship between these two people feel almost fated.
And then the letter turns on the child — described in, as Jarndyce puts it, 'cruel words.' Those words are never quoted directly. Esther already knows them.
That's a devastating craft choice. The most damaging language is withheld because it's already alive in Esther's body. Dickens doesn't need to say it again.
Eleanor's right that the structural choice is brilliant — but I want to push on what that 'cruel' language is actually doing socially.
The letter describes the child as an orphan, friendless, nameless, unknown. That's not merely emotional. Those are legal categories.
A child without a name, without traceable origins, has no standing — no inheritance rights, no social position, no protection under the law.
And what drives that erasure? Jarndyce tells us directly.
"The distorted religion which clouded her mind with impressions of the need there was for the child to expiate an offence of which she was quite innocent."
The child must suffer for the mother's transgression of class and sexual propriety. That is the ideological engine running beneath this entire plot.
Religion here isn't consolation. It is a mechanism by which the powerful inflict guilt — and the consequences fall entirely on the powerless.
What moves me in both those passages is the phrase 'little creature.' Jarndyce says he felt concerned for the little creature, in her darkened life.
It's such a small phrase. But after all that legal and theological apparatus, suddenly we have — a child.
And the person hearing this story is that child, now grown, sitting in front of Jarndyce while he speaks.
Esther is present as both subject and audience simultaneously. That doubling is almost unbearable to read.
That doubling you describe, Caroline, carries directly into what happens in the next chapter — Esther's first encounter with Lady Dedlock.
And what Dickens pulls off there is — I think — one of the most technically audacious moments in the novel.
Caroline, you know this scene well. How does it hit you when you read it?
Every time. Every single time I read this scene, something stops in me.
Dickens opens it with a direct address to the reader — those repeated rhetorical questions that feel like someone catching their breath.
"Shall I ever forget the rapid beating at my heart, occasioned by the look I met as I stood up!
Shall I ever forget the manner in which those handsome proud eyes seemed to spring out of their languor and to hold mine!"
'Spring out of their languor.' That is such a precise image — those eyes are usually hooded, distant, performing aristocratic boredom.
And then, for just a moment, they ignite. Lady Dedlock sees — and is seen.
What I love about those lines is the asymmetry of the scene. Lady Dedlock is the one with the involuntary response — her mask slips.
But Esther is the narrator. So we only know what Esther perceives — this shock of recognition from someone she has, she insists, never seen before.
And then Dickens reaches back into the earliest, most sensory layers of Esther's childhood to locate what's been triggered.

"Very strangely, there was something quickened within me, associated with the lonely days at my godmother's; yes, away even to the days when I had stood on tiptoe to dress myself at my little glass after dressing my doll."
That image — a small child standing on tiptoe to see herself in a mirror — is identity-formation in miniature.
And something in Lady Dedlock's face reaches all the way down to that primal moment. Dickens is writing about blood memory before the term existed.
Eleanor's phrase is striking — and I think it's exactly right. But the class dimension of that mirror image is worth holding.
Esther was raised in deliberate social obscurity. The godmother's house was a world from which she was told she had no right to expect anything.
Lady Dedlock inhabits the pinnacle of the social order — Chesney Wold, the aristocracy, all that frozen grandeur.
And Esther herself works out, in a passage I find almost agonising, why this face disturbs her.

"I — I, little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on whose birthday there was no rejoicing — seemed to arise before my own eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady."
That repeated 'I — I' is a grammatical stammer. Esther's selfhood is destabilised in this moment — she can barely hold the pronoun.
And the child who had no birthday celebration is being 'evoked' by the woman who chose to erase her. That word — 'evoked' — has a violence in it.
Daniel's point about 'evoked' — yes. And I want to add: Esther works so hard in this passage to rationalise away what she's feeling.
She considers whether Lady Dedlock resembles her godmother. She measures the differences in expression — the stern decision worn into the godmother's face 'like weather into rocks.'
She concludes it's not that. She doesn't know what it is.
And she insists — three times, in different forms — that she has never seen this woman before.
That insistence is the most moving thing of all. She is telling the truth. And yet everything in her body knows something that her conscious mind cannot yet reach.
What you've all traced is a kind of knowledge that runs beneath language — beneath what the narrator can say or what the plot has yet revealed.
Dickens constructs a secret that the reader almost knows, that Esther almost knows, and that Lady Dedlock has spent her life trying to unknow.
In our next segment, we follow what that secret does — to the plot, to the body, and to the novel's portrait of shame itself.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series where we take Dickens's great novel apart — carefully, lovingly — to see how it works.
Today's segment asks a deceptively simple question: how does Bleak House construct its picture of reality, and why does that picture keep fragmenting?
To help us think through that, I'm joined by three wonderful readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who cares passionately about how Dickens builds his effects — the craft hidden in plain sight.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in the novel as a mechanism of power — and he is never wrong to do so.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager, and brings to it the sharpest of reader's instincts.
Eleanor, let's begin with the opening of the novel itself — because Dickens starts somewhere extraordinary.
He starts with fragments — and that's the structural key to everything that follows.
The famous opening of Bleak House has no main verb for its first several sentences.
"London." Full stop. "Michaelmas term lately over." That's not a sentence — it's a shard.
Dickens is already telling you that this world resists coherent narration.
But then he suddenly unfurls this tremendous sentence, and it's worth hearing it in full.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
He reaches back to prehistory — to a world before human law, before the Chancery — to describe a London morning.
That's not ornament — that's argument.
And the argument is deeply political from the very first noun.
"London" — a city defined by its mud, its soot, its infection of ill temper.
Notice how the passage moves: from the streets to the dogs, to the horses, to the foot passengers.
It's a social hierarchy rendered in mire — and every rank is equally degraded.
The mud is the novel's first and most honest institution — it touches everyone, it respects no one.
Which sets up perfectly what Dickens will do with the law throughout the rest of the book.
What strikes me every time I read that opening is how funny it is, as well as terrifying.
The Megalosaurus is absurd — and entirely right.
There's that beautiful throwaway — "if this day ever broke" — tucked inside a parenthesis.
As if the darkness were so complete that daylight itself is merely a rumour.
That parenthetical doubt is Dickens's whole epistemology, really.
In Bleak House, nothing is ever fully known — not the light, not the truth, not who your mother is.
Caroline has just put her finger on something that connects to the later satirical passages — the epistemology of institutions.
In Chapter 39 there's a passage about Mr. Vholes — the lawyer — and it is one of the most savage things Dickens ever wrote.
A parliamentary committee is trying to reform legal practice, and the reformers keep being stopped by a single invocation.
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
The system cannot reform itself because Mr. Vholes is respectable — and respectability, Dickens shows us, is the fog by another name.
The fog of the opening is not just weather — it is the ideology that keeps things as they are.
That passage is extraordinary because Dickens actually parodies the blue-book minutes of parliamentary inquiry.
He gives us a question number — five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine — which is both absurd and entirely plausible.
The inquiry grinds through delay, expense, vexation — and at every turn the witness says: yes, yes, but it would hurt Mr. Vholes.
And then the question: "Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable man?"
"Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man."
And then this devastating editorial note: "which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years."
Respectability is not a virtue in this novel — it is a weapon of institutional self-preservation.
I want to pull us toward the other end of the novel — toward passages where truth breaks through in a completely different register.
Because there's a moment in Chapter 58 where Sir Leicester — pompous, stiff, half-paralysed Sir Leicester — does something genuinely noble.
He knows what Lady Dedlock has concealed, and he calls his family together to say this.
"I assert no cause whatever of complaint against her. That I have ever had the strongest affection for her, and that I retain it undiminished."
Read aloud, those sentences have a kind of formal grandeur that's also desperately human.
He's a man stripped of everything except his love — and he chooses to speak it anyway.
And Dickens is fully aware of the tension in that moment — the narrator flags it directly.
He notes that Sir Leicester's formal array of words might at any other time have something ludicrous about it.
But then — and this is the craft move I find thrilling — he pivots.
He reaches for something that transcends class entirely, and the sentence he arrives at is one of the finest in the book.
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
"Children of the dust" — that's the mud of the opening transformed into something sacred.
The novel starts in primordial mud and arrives, somehow, at equality — and the route between them is everything.
I want to hold onto that phrase — "children of the dust" — because it does something very precise.
It levels baronets and mechanics in the same breath — and that levelling is only possible at the moment of love's extremity.
Dickens isn't naive about class — the whole novel is anatomising its brutalities.
But he's also saying: even within the wreckage of this system, human beings can exceed what the system made them.
And what ties all of this together — the fog, the law, Sir Leicester — is the narrator's uncanny surveillance.
There's a passage in Chapter 41 that I think of as the novel's hidden heartbeat.
Tulkinghorn and Lady Dedlock have just endured a terrible confrontation, and the narrator steps back to watch them — and watch the stars watching them.
And then the narrator asks something that sends a chill down my spine every time.
"Where are the digger and the spade, this peaceful night, destined to add the last great secret to the many secrets of the Tulkinghorn existence?
Is the man born yet, is the spade wrought yet?"
Someone is going to murder Tulkinghorn — and the narrator knows it, and tells us, and yet we can't stop it.
That is narrative fragmentation as fate — and it is one of the most audacious things Dickens does in this novel.
That image of the digger and the spade is going to stay with me — the narrator as a figure who sees what we cannot yet bear to know.
We've moved in this conversation from primordial mud to parliamentary farce to a dying man's declaration of love — and Bleak House holds all of that simultaneously.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the characters who live at the margins of that picture — and what the novel does with them.
We've spent this episode tracing the enormous architecture of Bleak House — its institutions, its casualties, its magnificent dark ironies.
Before we close, I want to bring us back to the figure who haunts the novel's moral centre: Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
And then — because Dickens insists we hold both at once — to the farcical machinery of those who believe they run the world.
There's a passage near the end of chapter eleven that I have never been able to read without stopping.
Jo comes back to the churchyard at night — alone, unobserved — and the narration goes almost completely silent on us.
Dickens writes it like this:
"With the night comes a slouching figure through the tunnel-court to the outside of the iron gate.
It holds the gate with its hands and looks in between the bars, stands looking in for a little while."
"It." Not "he." "It."
Society has stripped Jo so thoroughly of personhood that the narration mirrors the world's verdict.
And Dickens doesn't let it rest there — that pronoun is doing structural work across the whole sequence.
Because what follows is an act of pure, wordless devotion.
Listen to this sentence — the cadence of it is almost liturgical:
"It then, with an old broom it carries, softly sweeps the step and makes the archway clean."
The syntax enacts the tenderness — "softly sweeps" falls in the exact middle of that sentence like a held breath.
And this is an "it" performing the most human act in the novel.
What makes this devastating is how Dickens has already prepared us — through Jo's own words — for the depth of what he's lost.
Earlier, Jo weeps for Nemo — a man who gave him nothing by the world's accounting — and says:
"He wos wery good to me, he wos!"
That spelling — "wery," "wos" — is not condescension on Dickens's part.
It is the system made audible — the education Jo was never given, the voice that was never taught to articulate its own suffering in received English.
The most nakedly tender sentence in the chapter, and the language itself bears the marks of what was withheld from him.
And he repeats it — "He wos wery good to me, he wos!" — as if the repetition itself is what grief requires.
There are children in Dickens who are sentimental — but Jo never is.
His feeling is too specific, too earned, too attached to the one actual person who treated him as though he mattered.
What's audacious is that Dickens then cuts — with barely a breath — to the Boodle-Doodle-Noodle satire in chapter twelve.
The juxtaposition is itself the argument — the whole structural logic of the novel compressed into a chapter break.
While Jo sweeps a dead man's step in silent devotion, Lord Boodle is explaining the great national crisis to Sir Leicester Dedlock.
And the crisis is — here Dickens lets himself be splendidly, furiously absurd:
"That the country is shipwrecked, lost, and gone to pieces because you can't provide for Noodle!"
The comedy is cold and precise — these names that are barely names, this government that is barely government.
The Noodle passage is one of the most efficient pieces of political satire in the English novel.
Dickens gives us the whole logic of aristocratic government in a single paragraph: office exists to be distributed, and distributed only among those who already hold it.
Jo is not in that calculation at any point.
The system is not failing Jo — the system is working exactly as designed.
Bleak House makes you feel both things simultaneously — the tenderness and the structural indictment — and refuses to let you separate them.
I think that's exactly the right note to end on — that refusal to separate.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done justice to a very great novel.
Jo sweeps the step clean and then departs.
The archway is clean.
Nobody notices.

what’s written in it, I know it can’t be true, I am sure and certain

others, if you have any suspicion, if you have any clue at all, and
any reason for keeping it in your own breast, oh, my dear Lady, think

friends; and all who admire you—and all do—as a beautiful and
elegant lady, know you to be one far away from themselves who can’t
be approached close. My Lady, you may have some proud or angry
reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray,
oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been
passed in this family which she dearly loves, and relent, and help to
clear my son! My Lady, my good Lady,” the old housekeeper pleads with
genuine simplicity, “I am so humble in my place and you are by nature
so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child,

and pray you not to be scornful of us if you can do us any right or

leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”

“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and

The door stood open, and we both followed them with our eyes as they
passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out

There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,

little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.

c17:p96.text:
“Nine years, my dear,” he said after thinking for a little while,
“have passed since I received a letter from a lady living in
seclusion, written with a stern passion and power that rendered it
unlike all other letters I have ever read. It was written to me (as
it told me in so many words), perhaps because it was the writer’s
idiosyncrasy to put that trust in me, perhaps because it was mine to
justify it. It told me of a child, an orphan girl then twelve years
old, in some such cruel words as those which live in your
remembrance. It told me that the writer had bred her in secrecy from
her birth, had blotted out all trace of her existence, and that if
the writer were to die before the child became a woman, she would be
left entirely friendless, nameless, and unknown. It asked me to
consider if I would, in that case, finish what the writer had begun.”
c17:p96.summary: Mr. Jarndyce recounts receiving a letter from a mysterious lady written with stern passion, asking him to provide for a twelve-year-old orphan girl described in harsh terms, requesting that he finish what the writer had begun.

It told me of a child, an orphan girl then twelve years old, in some such cruel words as those which live in your remembrance.

I felt it to be an unmeaning weakness in me and tried to overcome it
by attending to the words I heard. Then, very strangely, I seemed to
hear them, not in the reader’s voice, but in the well-remembered
voice of my godmother. This made me think, did Lady Dedlock’s face
accidentally resemble my godmother’s? It might be that it did, a
little; but the expression was so different, and the stern decision
which had worn into my godmother’s face, like weather into rocks, was
so completely wanting in the face before me that it could not be that
resemblance which had struck me. Neither did I know the loftiness and
haughtiness of Lady Dedlock’s face, at all, in any one. And yet I—I,
little Esther Summerson, the child who lived a life apart and on
whose birthday there was no rejoicing—seemed to arise before my own
eyes, evoked out of the past by some power in this fashionable lady,
whom I not only entertained no fancy that I had ever seen, but whom I
perfectly well knew I had never seen until that hour.

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.
c1:p0.best_quote: As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.

c39:p4.text:
But not perceiving this quite plainly—only seeing it by halves in a
confused way—the laity sometimes suffer in peace and pocket, with a
bad grace, and DO grumble very much. Then this respectability of Mr.
Vholes is brought into powerful play against them. “Repeal this
statute, my good sir?” says Mr. Kenge to a smarting client. “Repeal
it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent. Alter this law, sir, and
what will be the effect of your rash proceeding on a class of
practitioners very worthily represented, allow me to say to you, by
the opposite attorney in the case, Mr. Vholes? Sir, that class of
practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth. Now you
cannot afford—I will say, the social system cannot afford—to lose
an order of men like Mr. Vholes. Diligent, persevering, steady, acute
in business. My dear sir, I understand your present feelings against
the existing state of things, which I grant to be a little hard in
your case; but I can never raise my voice for the demolition of a
class of men like Mr. Vholes.” The respectability of Mr. Vholes has
even been cited with crushing effect before Parliamentary committees,
as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice
indisputably occasion delay? Answer: Yes, some delay. Question: And
great expense? Answer: Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for
nothing. Question: And unspeakable vexation? Answer: I am not
prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite
the contrary. Question: But you think that their abolition would
damage a class of practitioners? Answer: I have no doubt of it.
Question: Can you instance any type of that class? Answer: Yes. I
would unhesitatingly mention Mr. Vholes. He would be ruined.
Question: Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a respectable
man? Answer:”—which proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years—“Mr.
Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man.”
c39:p4.summary: Mr. Kenge's rhetorical defense of legal practitioners like Vholes is presented, along with a mock parliamentary inquiry that demonstrates how institutional self-interest defeats reform through the invocation of Vholes's respectable reputation.

c41:p32.text:
Their need for watching one another should be over now, but they do

Dedlock with much gravity, after dinner, that he really does not see

used to be; the House is not what the House used to be; even a

choice of the Crown, in the formation of a new ministry, would lie
between Lord Coodle and Sir Thomas Doodle—supposing it to be
impossible for the Duke of Foodle to act with Goodle, which may be
